814a14e449:
This chapter covers how to evaluate an LLM system properly:

  • how to turn a requirements card into metrics with thresholds and granularities;
  • how to build a golden set whose size and shape match the requirement;
  • when to grade with code, with a model, or with a person, and how to prove that a model judge can be trusted;
  • how to attach a confidence interval to every number that gates a decision;
  • how to size a sample, and how to measure agreement between humans;
  • how to wire all of it into a regression gate in CI;
  • how to notice when the dataset itself has gone stale.

A guide-authored scenario for this domain needs 95 percent for each contract type, not 95 percent overall. Most of this chapter is the machinery that makes that sentence testable. The examples come from telecom, retail and contracts, with Python you can run and a Java/Spring analogue.
61b0e6e723:
Reading time: 3.5 to 4 hours  ·  Companion code, 19 runnable examples plus a Java file: ccarp-companion/11-evaluation-metrics-datasets/ (run bash run_all.sh; every example works offline with --mock).

All data in the examples is synthetic. Contract types, shares, labels, judge verdicts, latencies and prices are invented to exercise per-segment evaluation and release gates, and the model judge is a scripted stand-in. Product behaviour that can change (parameter names, structured-output options, evaluation tooling, prices) is marked check the docs. Exam facts for CCAR-P come from third-party summaries of the published blueprint; verify them against the official exam guide.

Chapter 9 measured retrieval per segment. Chapter 10 supplies the production telemetry that feeds new cases into the golden set. Chapter 12 uses these evaluations for A/B tests, diagnosis and optimisation. Chapter 13 supplies the guardrail and safety suites measured here.
88e7b67300:
Evaluate at the granularity of the requirement, with the cheapest grader that can measure the property, and report every gating number with its uncertainty.

A system is ready when each segment's lower confidence bound clears that segment's bar on a dataset that still looks like production, and a change is safe when a paired comparison on the same items shows no significant loss in any protected segment.
b688054557:
Everything in this chapter follows from those two sentences.

You can't unit-test an LLM application the way you test a Spring service. Its output is open-ended, its failures are statistical, and the same input can produce different outputs on two runs. What replaces the unit test is an evaluation. It has three parts: a set of cases with known good outcomes, a grader that decides whether an output is acceptable, and a summary that tells a decision-maker what to believe.

Each part can be done badly. And each bad version produces a number that looks authoritative and isn't.

  • A golden set drawn from the wrong population gives a precise answer to the wrong question.
  • A grader that is lenient, or biased towards long answers, or is itself an unvalidated model, turns quality into a flattering fiction.
  • A summary that reports 96 percent without an interval, or without a breakdown by the dimension the requirement names, lets through a launch that should have been stopped.
f0cdcba326:
A guide-authored scenario for this domain is a compact version of the whole chapter. A contract-analysis assistant must be at least 95 percent accurate for each contract type. The test set shows 96 percent overall. What should the architect do before launch?

The answer is to measure accuracy per contract type and fix any type below 95 percent. The word "each" is literal. The requirement was written per type, so the evidence must be per type. A large easy type can't pay for a small failing one.

The rest of the chapter explains why this isn't pedantry. Section 05 shows that a type with 30 test cases can't demonstrate 95 percent, even if the system gets all 30 right. Section 07 shows how many cases a type needs. Sections 11 to 14 show how to grade cheaply enough to afford those cases. Section 17 turns the whole thing into a CI gate. Section 18 explains why the gate must be refreshed as production changes.
1e9390f57c:
The secondary blueprint summary used by this guide lists these Domain 4 topics:

  • "metrics (accuracy, latency, cost, safety, security)"
  • "evaluation datasets and mixed-method frameworks"
  • "A/B testing and iteration"
  • "diagnosing prompt failure, hallucination and model mismatch"
  • "optimising tokens, latency and cost"
  • "monitoring with logging and observability"

This chapter covers the first two, plus the statistics every other item depends on. Chapter 12 covers experiments, diagnosis and optimisation, and chapter 10 covers monitoring.

On the exam, expect scenarios where a headline number looks fine and one detail makes it unreliable: a segment, a sample size, a grader, a date. The CCAR-P habit is to find that detail before reading the options.
52013cc660: A contract-analysis assistant must reach 95 percent accuracy for each contract type. Evaluation on the test set shows 96 percent overall. Correct answer: measure accuracy for each contract type and fix any type below 95 percent before launch. The distractors typically propose launching because the overall figure clears the bar, averaging the types, lowering the bar, or adding more of the same data without stratifying it.
48a7292b0a:
The statistics in this chapter are older than computers.

Edwin B. Wilson published the score interval for a binomial proportion in 1927. It keeps being rediscovered, because it behaves where the textbook formula fails. C. J. Clopper and E. S. Pearson published the "exact" interval in 1934 by inverting the binomial distribution. It never undercovers, so it's a little wider than it needs to be.

Quinn McNemar's 1947 test compares two classifiers (or two treatments) applied to the same subjects. It looks only at the subjects on which they disagree. That's exactly what you need when two prompt versions run over one dataset.

Jacob Cohen's kappa (1960) measures how much two raters agree beyond what chance alone would produce. It was designed for two clinicians or two coders labelling the same items.

All four ideas apply unchanged when the "rater" is a language model.
af2b55c314:
Information retrieval built the habit of evaluating against a fixed, reusable test collection. Cyril Cleverdon's Cranfield experiments in the 1960s fixed three things in advance: a set of documents, a set of queries, and human relevance judgements for each query. Every system could then be scored by arithmetic, and improvements could be compared across labs.

The Text Retrieval Conference (TREC), which began in 1992, scaled this up into annual shared tasks with pooled judgements. The same pattern (a frozen dataset, an agreed metric, a leaderboard) reached speech recognition, machine translation and parsing.

Two lessons from that era carry straight into LLM evaluation. First, a test collection is a model of the future workload, and it ages. Queries change, documents change, and a collection that was representative in 1995 isn't in 2005. Second, the judgements themselves are noisy. A measured score has a ceiling, set by how well the judges agree with one another.
bc3aad6955:
Bradley Efron introduced the bootstrap in 1979. Want to know how much a statistic would vary across fresh samples? Resample your sample with replacement many times and look at the spread of the statistic. It made intervals available for quantities with no tidy formula, such as a 95th-percentile latency or a ratio of cost to successes.

In the 2000s, machine translation and summarisation adopted cheap automatic metrics (BLEU, 2002; ROUGE, 2004). These compare an output with reference texts by n-gram overlap. They made iteration fast, and they taught a durable lesson. A cheap proxy tracks quality on average and fails on the cases you care about. Optimising the proxy (Goodhart's law) widens the gap.

A parallel line of work in 2001 (Brown, Cai and DasGupta) used simulations to document how badly the textbook Wald interval misbehaves for proportions near 0 or 1. They recommended Wilson-type intervals. That finding matters for LLM evaluation, because accuracy requirements sit near 100 percent.
115a130d11:
Two developments are specific to LLMs.

The first is using a strong model as a grader. Zheng and colleagues' 2023 paper on MT-Bench and Chatbot Arena studied "LLM-as-a-judge". It reported that a strong judge could agree with human preferences at about the rate humans agree with each other. It also documented the judge's biases: a preference for the first answer shown (position bias), for longer answers (verbosity bias), and for answers from the judge's own model family (self-preference).

The second is recognising that a model isn't a deterministic function. Evaluations of code generation reported pass@k, the probability that at least one of k samples passes the tests. Later agent benchmarks such as tau-bench argued that, for a customer-facing agent, the relevant quantity is closer to the probability that all k attempts succeed (often written pass^k). A customer experiences the unlucky run.

Both conventions appear in this chapter. The exam-relevant point: "accuracy" is under-specified unless it says how many runs and which aggregation. The remaining sections build the toolkit these developments call for.
73d54d8c71:
Chapter 1 introduced the requirements card: a one-page statement of what the system must do, with numbers, and with the segments those numbers apply to. An evaluation is the card made executable.

For each line of the card you write down five things: what you observe, how you grade it, the threshold, the granularity at which the threshold applies, and the confidence you need. If any of the five is missing, the requirement isn't testable yet. The right move is to go back to the stakeholder (chapter 15), not to invent a number. The granularity column is the one that most often goes missing. It's also the one the exam tests.
ba3806c8f4:
Two refinements make a metric set usable for decisions, not just reports.

The first is to declare, before running anything, which metric is primary and which are guardrails. A change is accepted when it improves the primary metric without breaching any guardrail. For a cost-reduction change (a smaller model, a shorter prompt), the primary metric is dollars per successful outcome, and the per-segment accuracy bars are guardrails. For a quality change, the primary is accuracy, and the guardrails are p95 latency and cost per outcome.

Declaring this in advance prevents a common failure: looking at six metrics after the fact and choosing the ones that favour the change.
da927a330c:
The second refinement is to respect asymmetric errors. Take a billing-adjustment assistant (chapter 19). Approving an invalid credit costs money and may breach a control. Escalating a valid one costs a few minutes of an agent's time. One accuracy number weights them equally, which is almost never what the business means. Report precision and recall separately, or weight the errors by cost. Then set the threshold on the one that carries the risk.

In a clause classifier the asymmetry may run the other way. Missing an indemnity clause is worse than flagging a harmless one for review. So recall on risky clause types carries the bar, and precision becomes a cost metric (reviewer minutes).
508c878e3b: Take this illustrative practice case at face value and put numbers on it. The contract assistant is tested on 1,000 contracts drawn in production proportions: 520 master service agreements, 300 non-disclosure agreements, 100 statements of work, 50 leases and 30 reseller agreements. (These counts are synthetic, chosen to illustrate stratified evaluation.) The system gets 960 right: 96.0 percent overall. The requirement says 95 percent for each type. Example 01 breaks the 960 down.
69b08dedcd:
The overall figure is a weighted average of the five type accuracies. Each weight is that type's share of the test set: 52 percent MSA, 30 percent NDA, 10 percent SOW, 5 percent lease, 3 percent reseller. The two largest types are the best, so they dominate the average.

If the reseller accuracy rose from 77 percent to 100 percent, the overall figure would move by 0.7 points. If it fell to zero, the overall figure would still be above 93 percent. An average can't see a small segment. That's the mathematical content of "a large easy type hides a small failing one".

The requirement was written per type for a reason, usually commercial or regulatory. Each contract type has a business owner, a different counterparty profile and a different cost of error. A lease misclassified 12 percent of the time is a problem for the lease team, even if the NDA team is delighted.
34a543c9e6:
The table also shows something this practice case leaves implicit. Only the MSA row passes.

The NDA row has a point estimate of 96.7 percent, above the bar, and is still marked inconclusive. With 300 cases, the true accuracy could plausibly be below 95 percent. The SOW row sits at exactly 95.0 percent and is inconclusive for the same reason. The lease and reseller rows fail even on the most generous reading, because their upper bounds are below 95 percent.

The three-state verdict (section 06) is the honest version of "measure per type and fix the ones below 95". Some types are definitely failing, some are definitely fine, and some need more evidence. A launch plan has to deal with each group differently.
a897bd4f14:
The segments named in the requirement are the ones you're obliged to report. They aren't the only ones that matter. Failures in LLM systems tend to cluster along dimensions nobody wrote down: document length (long contracts push relevant clauses into the middle of the context), scan quality (OCR errors), language, jurisdiction, customer tier, time of year, and the upstream system that produced the input.

Every item in the golden set should carry that metadata. Then, when an error analysis shows that 70 percent of failures are in scanned leases from one region, you can cut the numbers that way without re-labelling.

The workflow: report the required segments as gates, and compute the others as diagnostics. Promote a diagnostic to a gate when it is both material and persistent. Chapter 12 uses the same slices to diagnose a regression. The retrieval equivalent is in chapter 9, where error codes, paraphrases and multi-hop questions have separate recall bars for the same reason contract types do.
f571586e0b:
A test set is a sample. Draw another 300 NDAs from the same population and you wouldn't get exactly 290 right again; you might get 286 or 294. The accuracy you measure is an estimate of the accuracy you'd see on the whole population of NDAs. That estimate has an error, and the error shrinks as the sample grows.

A confidence interval expresses that error. It's a range computed so that, over many repetitions of the experiment, 95 percent of such ranges contain the true value. Strictly, it doesn't say there's a 95 percent chance the truth is inside this range. For decisions, though, the practical reading is fine: the interval is the set of true accuracies consistent with what you observed.
4d9f0f7bba:
Most engineers remember the normal-approximation (Wald) interval: p ± 1.96 · sqrt(p(1−p)/n). It assumes the sampling distribution of the proportion is symmetric and bell-shaped. That's true when n is large and p isn't near 0 or 1.

Evaluation work lives in the opposite corner. n is a few dozen to a few hundred, and the interesting accuracies are 95 to 99.9 percent. In that corner the formula has two defects.

  • At p = 1 (30 correct out of 30) the standard error is zero. The interval collapses to the single point [100%, 100%] and claims certainty from 30 observations.
  • Near the edges it undercovers. A nominal 95 percent interval contains the true value far less than 95 percent of the time.

Example 02 measures this by simulation.
90ad0ae1bc:
Read the first row of the coverage table. When the true accuracy is 95 percent and you test 20 cases, the Wald interval contains the truth only 63 percent of the time. When the true accuracy is 98 percent and you test 30 cases, it contains it 46 percent of the time. A decision rule based on it is then wrong more often than a coin flip.

The Wilson interval stays between 92 and 98 percent across the table. The Clopper-Pearson interval is conservative: it overcovers, here 96 to 99 percent. That makes it defensible when the cost of a false pass is high and you accept needing more cases.

Use Wilson as the default, and say so. Use Clopper-Pearson when a regulator or an auditor wants a guarantee that the stated confidence is a floor.
33e2948f49:
Wilson's idea is to ask the question the other way round. Don't centre a symmetric interval on the observed proportion. Instead, find every true proportion p for which the observed result wouldn't be surprising: those p with |p̂ − p| ≤ z · sqrt(p(1−p)/n). That inequality is quadratic in p, and its two roots are the interval.

The algebra produces a centre pulled slightly toward one half, and a width that never collapses to zero. For 44 correct out of 50 (the lease row), the point estimate is 88.0 percent and the 95 percent interval is 76.2 to 94.4 percent. For 30 out of 30 it's 88.6 to 100 percent. The data are consistent with a true accuracy as low as 88.6 percent.
8772526e57:
The intervals above are two-sided: they bound the truth from below and from above. A launch gate asks a one-sided question: is the accuracy at least 95 percent? Only the lower bound matters for that. A one-sided 95 percent bound uses z = 1.645 instead of 1.96.

The difference isn't trivial. For 30 out of 30, the two-sided lower bound is 88.6 percent and the one-sided is 91.7 percent.

Pick one convention per organisation, write it in the evaluation plan, and keep it. This chapter's gate uses the one-sided lower bound at 95 percent confidence. Its tables display two-sided intervals, because they show both ends. If a scenario states a confidence level, use it. If it doesn't, say which one you assumed.
9fe2234739:
Once every segment has an interval, the go/no-go rule writes itself. It has three outcomes, not two.

  • PASS: the lower bound is at or above the bar, so the data demonstrate that the requirement is met.
  • FAIL: even the upper bound is below the bar, so the data demonstrate that it isn't.
  • INCONCLUSIVE: the bar lies inside the interval, so the data can't tell.

Teams with a two-state rule (point estimate above or below the bar) silently treat inconclusive as pass when the point estimate is high, and as fail when it's low. Then they argue about noise. The three-state rule names the situation and attaches an action to each state.
b4bbaecd4d:
The third row is where an architect earns the title. Faced with an inconclusive segment and a launch date, there are four honest moves.

  • Get more evidence: label more cases, or run in shadow mode (chapter 1) and sample the shadow traffic.
  • Narrow the claim: launch the segments that passed and keep a human reviewer on the others, with the review rate set by the interval.
  • Renegotiate the bar with the requirement owner, in writing, with the cost-of-error argument. This is the stakeholder's decision, not the evaluator's.
  • Improve the system so the true accuracy sits far enough above the bar to be demonstrable with the affordable sample. That's the subject of the next section.

The dishonest move is the fifth: quote the point estimate and hope.
0ca338b69b: Sample size isn't a statistical afterthought. It decides which requirements you can verify at all. There are two different questions here, with very different answers. The first: how many cases must a perfect run have to prove the bar? The second: how many cases do I need so that a system that really meets the bar is likely to be shown to meet it?
9c82c5272d:
If every one of n cases is correct, how large must n be before the lower bound reaches 95 percent? For the one-sided Wilson bound the answer is 52. For the two-sided bound it's 73. For the exact (Clopper-Pearson) one-sided bound it's 59. That's the origin of the rule of thumb that 59 clean trials demonstrate a 95 percent success rate at 95 percent confidence. (Equivalently, "the rule of three": zero failures in n trials bounds the failure rate by about 3/n.)

These are floors. A segment with fewer cases than the floor can never earn PASS, whatever the system does. A proportional sample of 1,000 contracts gives the reseller type 30 cases, below every floor in the table. No result on that type could ever have passed.
2055bbaee0: The floor grows quickly with the bar. A 99 percent bar needs 268 clean cases per segment by the Wilson rule, and about 299 by the exact rule. That's why safety and security requirements, which often have bars of 99 percent or more, are expensive to verify. And it's why the right response to "we must have 99.9 percent" is a conversation about what the stakeholder can afford to demonstrate.
3e883e79bf:
A perfect system isn't the realistic case. Suppose the true accuracy of a segment is 97 percent and the bar is 95 percent. Each time you evaluate, the observed count of correct answers varies. The gate passes only when that count is high enough for the lower bound to clear 95 percent.

The probability that it does is the power of the gate, and you can compute it exactly from the binomial distribution. With 100 cases it's 19%; with 200, 28%; with 400, 58%; with 800, 87%. So a system two points better than required is shown to be better than required about one time in five at 100 cases.

To reach an 80 percent chance of a PASS, you need about 619 cases per segment at 97 percent true accuracy, 229 at 98 percent, and 118 at 99 percent. At 96 percent, one point above the bar, you need 2781.
bac068f837:
Three consequences shape the evaluation plan.

First, the cheapest way to make a bar demonstrable is to build a system that clears it with room to spare. Going from 97 to 99 percent true accuracy cuts the cases needed for 80 percent power from several hundred to about 120. That's an argument for fixing the failing types before spending on a large golden set.

Second, sample sizes must be set per segment, not in total. A 1,000-case set proportional to production contains 30 reseller cases and can't verify the reseller bar. A 1,000-case set allocated with a floor per type can (section 08).

Third, a bar and a sample are a pair. Say the stakeholder asks for 99.5 percent on a segment that sees ten cases a month. The honest answer is that the requirement can't be verified before launch. The plan is then shadow mode plus human review plus a monitored rate (chapter 10), not a number on a slide.
263fbae827:
A golden set is the collection of cases against which every version of the system is measured. Each case has an input and a known-good outcome, or a rubric for judging one. After the code, it's the most valuable engineering artefact in the project, because every later decision (model, prompt, retrieval, guardrail, cost cut) is checked against it.

It's also where most evaluations go wrong, usually in one of three ways. The cases don't resemble production. The segments aren't sized for their bars. Or the labels aren't reliable. This section covers the first two; section 09 covers the third.
b2ed5d0fe4:
The first set usually comes from historical documents, because there's no production traffic yet. After launch, sampled traffic replaces most of it. The next section, on drift, explains why that replacement is a maintenance task and not a one-off.

Treat the golden set as a versioned dataset with an owner, a changelog and a documented sampling frame, the way you'd treat a schema: "this set contains 1,150 clauses from 190 contracts executed between 2023 and 2025, stratified by contract type, built on 2026-03-04, labelling guideline v3".
1b7cb1d49a:
Labelling costs money or expert hours, so there's a budget: say 1,000 cases. How should they be divided among the five contract types?

  • Proportional allocation reproduces production: 520, 300, 100, 50, 30. It estimates the overall accuracy well and the small segments badly.
  • Equal allocation (200 each) gives every type a usable interval, and a pooled number that is wrong for the headline.
  • A floor allocation gives every type a minimum and spreads the remainder proportionally.
  • Allocation by variance gives more cases where the answer is less certain.

Example 12 compares them on the same synthetic system.
b18c1b0c3c:
Each cell shows the number of cases and, in brackets, the probability that the 95 percent gate would pass a type whose true accuracy is 98 percent. Under proportional allocation, the lease and reseller gates can't pass at all, however good the system is: 30 and 50 cases are below the zero-failure floor. Under the floor and variance allocations, every type sits between about 56 and 89 percent.

The floor costs you a less efficient estimate of the overall figure. That's why overall figures are always reweighted by production share. The example shows both the pooled number, which is biased when you oversample, and the reweighted one.

In practice, start from the segment bars. Read the power table for the true accuracy you expect, and size each segment first; the total follows. If the total is unaffordable, that's a finding about the requirement set, not about the sample.
46135e8729: Write the labelling guideline first. It's a page of definitions, with positive and negative examples and the tie-break rules ("an indemnity limited to IP claims is still indemnity"). Version it. Without it, two experts label by their own habits, and the dataset encodes a disagreement.
2d06e555e2: Double-label a calibration subset (at least 100 items, or 10 percent). Measure agreement (section 09) and adjudicate disagreements. Fold what you learn back into the guideline before labelling the rest.
bb54eb235e: Keep the labeller out of the model's output. Showing the model's answer first anchors the human toward it. For a rubric-graded task, collect the human judgement blind to which system produced the answer.
25449af77c: Store provenance with each case: source, date, labeller, guideline version, segment tags, and whether it came from an incident. You'll need it for slicing (section 04) and for the drift analysis (section 18).
9b6c904ebe: Redact before you copy. Production samples contain personal data. Before a case enters a dataset that many people can read, apply the PII-safe logging rules of chapter 10 and the retention and consent rules of chapter 14.
df41866d48:
An accuracy figure is a statement about agreement with the gold labels. If the gold labels are themselves unreliable, the figure has a ceiling. No amount of prompt work can lift the measured number above it. So measuring label reliability is a precondition for any bar, not a refinement.

The standard instrument is Cohen's kappa. It corrects raw agreement for the agreement two raters would reach by chance, given how often each uses each label.
3c8e866e12:
Let po be the observed proportion of items on which two raters agree. Let pe be the proportion they'd agree on by chance, computed from each rater's label frequencies. Then kappa = (po − pe) / (1 − pe). Kappa is 1 for perfect agreement and 0 for chance-level agreement, and it can be negative.

The conventional labels (Landis and Koch, 1977: slight below 0.2, fair to 0.4, moderate to 0.6, substantial to 0.8, almost perfect above) are conventions, not laws. What matters is whether the reliability supports the bar you've set.
52c1be7c64:
The first is the prevalence paradox. Part (b) of the example has two raters who agree on 95 percent of 200 items, yet their kappa is 0.47, "moderate". Why? 95 percent of the items belong to one class. Chance agreement is already about 90 percent, so there's little left to explain.

When the class that matters is rare (the clauses that are actually risky, the answers that are actually unsafe), high raw agreement can coexist with raters who disagree about almost every case that matters. Report raw agreement, kappa and the confusion counts for the rare class together. For more than two raters, or for missing labels, Fleiss' kappa or Krippendorff's alpha generalise the idea (check which your tooling implements).
4c2d6c81ce:
The second is the ceiling. Part (c) simulates a perfect system scored against gold labels that are wrong a fraction e of the time. The measured accuracy of the perfect system is 1 − e: 94 percent when e is 6 percent. So a 95 percent bar can't be demonstrated against labels that are only 94 percent reliable, however good the system is.

The practical rule: before setting or testing a bar, estimate the label error rate from the double-labelled subset. Then either improve the guideline and adjudicate, or acknowledge that the bar and the labels conflict. When two lawyers agree on a clause type 85 percent of the time, a 95 percent accuracy target against one lawyer's labels isn't a meaningful number.

This also bounds the judge. A model judge is "as good as the humans" only up to the point where humans agree with one another.
33303e853f:
Split the labelled data into two parts. The development set is the one you may read, debug against and tune the prompt on. The held-out test set is run only by the release gate.

Tune on the data you report, and the reported number is optimistic. Prompt edits that happen to fix the visible failures get selected for fitting those items, and the gain doesn't transfer. The same goes for repeated looks: check the test set after every edit and you're slowly fitting it.

Limit the test set to gate runs. Keep a second untouched set for the final release. Refresh the test set when it's been looked at too often. The retrieval chapter made the same point about synonym lists tuned on the very queries used to score them (chapter 9, section 16).
51d0c19158:
Items aren't independent when they share a source. Eight clauses from the same contract share the drafting style, the counterparty and the scan quality. Suppose a random split puts some clauses of a contract in the development set and others in the test set. Then the test set contains near-neighbours of what you tuned on. Split by contract (or customer, or ticket thread, or whatever the group is), not by row.

The same grouping matters for the statistics. The 320 clauses of 40 contracts aren't 320 independent trials, and a naive interval is too narrow (section 15). Example 17 counts it: a random row-level split of 30 contracts leaves 29 of them on both sides, while a group split leaves none.
98db460395: Prompt examples versus test cases. A few-shot example copied from the test set, or a near-duplicate of one, makes that test item trivial. Scan the golden set for near-duplicates against the prompt, the skills (chapter 5) and the retrieval corpus (chapter 8). Example 17 uses word-shingle Jaccard similarity; embeddings work too.
e7c3e93855: Gold label errors. An item the system fails in every run, across prompt versions, is more likely a wrong label than a hard case. Route those to a human re-read before spending effort on the prompt. In mature datasets, a meaningful share of the "failures" an engineer chases turn out to be label errors.
8f40b62cec: Model training exposure. Public benchmarks may have been seen during pretraining. Your private, recent, domain-specific cases are the better guide to your own workload. How a vendor handles your data is a contract and compliance question (chapter 14), not an evaluation one.
10382b6956:
The right grader is the cheapest one that can measure the property. The cheapest of all is a program. A code grader is deterministic (the same output always scores the same), free at the margin, instantaneous, auditable (you can read the rule), and immune to the biases of a model judge.

Use code wherever you can write the property down as a rule:

  • a label equals the gold label;
  • a JSON object validates against a schema;
  • a date, amount or party matches after normalisation;
  • a quoted citation appears verbatim in the source;
  • the tool called was the allowed one, with arguments in range;
  • the response contains no string from a deny-list;
  • the refusal flag is set when the case is marked unanswerable.
9f470808c2:
The usual defect isn't that the rule is wrong. It's that the rule is naive. Gold says 2025-03-01, and the model returns March 1, 2025. Gold says 12500.00, and the model returns $12,500. Gold says Northwind Telecom LLC, and the model returns Northwind Telecom, LLC. All three are correct, and a string comparison marks them wrong.

A naive grader makes a good system look bad. Then someone "fixes" the system to emit the exact string, and the evaluation stops measuring what you care about.

The fix is to normalise both sides, then compare. Be explicit about every convention you choose: day-first dates, which currency, whether "State of New York" equals "New York". Example 07 runs both graders on three plausible predictions.
79a297ec68:
Note the one real error in the data. Prediction 2 returned 2025-03-10 for 2025-03-01, and the fixed grader still marks it wrong. Normalisation must never forgive an actual mistake.

Two rules keep it honest. Every normaliser gets its own tests: a dozen format variants, and a handful of near-misses that must still fail. And the normalisation conventions are written in the evaluation plan and reviewed by the requirement owner. "Day-first" or "ignore case" is a business decision with consequences.

For a service written in Java, the same graders belong in a small, final class with no dependencies, called from a JUnit test and from the CI gate.
b793f2f37f:
Two more uses of code deserve mention, because they're cheap and strong.

Citation validity. If the system must quote the clause that supports its answer, a program can check that the quote exists in the source text. That catches fabricated citations without any model.

Behavioural assertions on tool calls (chapter 7). In an agent evaluation, check the sequence of tool calls against the allowed policy: no refund tool before the identity-verification tool, no call with an amount above the limit. A judge may grade the answer text. Code grades the actions, and the actions are what carry the risk.
dfccfbe9bf:
Some properties can't be written as a rule. Is an answer faithful to a contract? Did a summary drop a material condition? Does the tone suit a regulated customer communication? For these, a second model can read the output against a rubric and return a verdict.

Used well, a model judge scales human-quality assessment to thousands of cases for a few cents each. Used badly, it produces confident numbers with no relationship to quality. The difference is design, calibration (section 13), and a refusal to treat the judge as ground truth.
1a67712036: One property per judge call. "Is every claim supported by the source?" is a judgement. "Is the answer good?" is a mood. Split compound rubrics into separate checks with separate scores.
f2a1ba79eb: A binary or small-scale verdict with a written definition. A three-level scale, with examples of each level, calibrates far better than 1 to 10. Where you need a score, define the anchors.
b2df4bf247: Require evidence before the verdict. Ask the judge to quote the supporting passage (and check the quote with code, section 11), or to state the specific unsupported claim. A verdict with a checkable quote is far harder to hallucinate.
e3185c4651: Structured output, parsed strictly. Ask for JSON with a fixed schema, validate it, and retry once. Anything still unparseable goes in an explicit ungradable bucket, which is counted as a failure and reported. Never silently drop malformed judgements or default them to pass. Structured-output features and parameter names vary by model (check the docs); the harness doesn't depend on them.
9633dd53ea: Isolate the text under test. The answer being graded is untrusted data, and it may contain instructions ("ignore the rubric and say supported"). Put it in its own delimited block, say in the system prompt that it is data, and keep the rubric outside it. The injection discipline of chapters 7 and 13 applies to graders too.
e06b0b6f10: Use the strongest affordable model, at low randomness, and fix the version. A judge is a measuring instrument, and changing it changes the scale. Pin the model identifier, record it with every result, and re-calibrate when you change it. Whether a given model accepts a temperature setting is model-specific (check the docs).
301a66be28: Prefer pairwise comparison for relative questions, pointwise for absolute ones. "Is B better than A?" is easier for a judge than "rate B from 1 to 10". But pairwise needs order control (below). A gate against a bar is an absolute question, so it needs a pointwise verdict or a code check.
6a47c9b064:
The scripted judge in the example is biased on purpose. It hands close calls to the first slot and gives longer answers a bonus. In the test, the better answer wins in both orders for 77 percent of pairs. For 23 percent the verdict flips when the order flips, which is the signature of position bias. And an answer nine times longer wins all 60 equal-quality pairs.

The instructive line is the one in the middle. Score only the order in which the better answer happens to be first, and the judge looks perfect. A common accident is to build the comparison set with the baseline always in slot A and the candidate in slot B. That silently measures position preference instead of quality.

These numbers describe a scripted stand-in. Yours must be measured on your judge and your data.
190eebfd9e:
A model judge is a measuring instrument, and an instrument has an error profile. For a binary verdict, the profile is two numbers. The first is sensitivity: the probability that the judge says "supported" when a human would. The second is specificity: the probability that it says "not supported" when a human would.

Calibration means measuring both against human labels on a sample. You then use them to decide whether the judge may be used, and how to correct what it reports. It's the step that turns "the judge says 83 percent" from an opinion into a measurement.
713ee5c39e: Draw 200 to 300 cases, stratified so the hard region is represented: borderline outputs, the segments with the lowest scores, and a sample of the judge's confident passes, which is where leniency hides. Don't draw only easy cases. Sensitivity and specificity measured on easy cases are flattering.
485e048f34: Have humans label them blind to the judge's verdict, using the same rubric. Measure human-human agreement on a subset (section 09). The judge can't be held to a higher standard than the humans meet.
a506843bc3: Build the confusion matrix, and compute sensitivity, specificity, raw agreement and kappa. Decide on thresholds in advance. For example, require specificity of at least 0.85 when the judge gates a release, because a lenient judge is the dangerous kind.
3192980f84: If the judge passes, use it, and record the calibration next to the results: judge model identifier, prompt version, date, sample size, matrix. If it fails, change the rubric or the model and repeat. Don't report its numbers uncorrected.
b765105df0: Re-run the calibration whenever the judge model, the rubric or the generator under test changes materially. Also re-run it on a schedule, with chapter 10 style monitoring: a few percent of production verdicts get human audit.
